items.followUp: How are conclusions drawn from the results of a biological experiment?

rubric.why: Award for explaining how experimental findings are presented or organised.
rubric.description: Results are summarised in an organised form, such as tables, graphs or charts.
rubric.how: Look for a named way of organising or presenting results; accept an equivalent method.

rubric.why: Award for explaining that results are interpreted to reach a conclusion, often in relation to the hypothesis.
rubric.description: The summarised results are interpreted to draw a conclusion about the hypothesis.
rubric.how: Look for both interpretation/conclusion and its link to the hypothesis or results.

modelAnswer: Experimental results are organised and summarised, for example in tables, graphs or charts.
The results are interpreted to draw a conclusion and decide whether they support the hypothesis.

items.followUp: Define exocytosis and state what happens during this process.

rubric.why: Award for defining endocytosis as the uptake of material into a cell by the cell membrane.
rubric.description: Endocytosis is the process by which a cell takes in material by enclosing it in a membrane-bound vesicle.
rubric.how: Look for uptake into the cell and enclosure by the cell membrane or a vesicle.

rubric.why: Award for naming both types and identifying what each takes in.
rubric.description: Its two types are phagocytosis, which takes in solid particles, and pinocytosis, which takes in liquids.
rubric.how: Look for both type names; accept a correct solid/liquid distinction.

modelAnswer: Endocytosis is the process by which a cell takes in material by enclosing it in a vesicle formed from its cell membrane.
Its two types are phagocytosis (uptake of solid particles) and pinocytosis (uptake of liquids).

items.followUp: What is a leucoplast, and where is it commonly found?

rubric.why: Award for identifying chromoplasts as coloured plastids containing pigments.
rubric.description: A chromoplast is a coloured plastid containing pigments.
rubric.how: Look for the terms plastid and colour or pigment.

rubric.why: Award for stating where chromoplasts occur or what colours they contribute to plant parts.
rubric.description: Chromoplasts occur especially in flowers and fruits and give them colour.
rubric.how: Look for flowers or fruits, or an equivalent plant part, and the role of giving colour.

modelAnswer: A chromoplast is a coloured plastid that contains pigments.
It is commonly found in flowers and fruits, where it gives them colour.

items.followUp: State the two parts of a scientific name and the rules for writing them.

rubric.why: Award for stating that binomial nomenclature gives each organism a two-word scientific name made of genus and species.
rubric.description: Binomial nomenclature is the system of giving each organism a two-word scientific name: genus and species.
rubric.how: Look for two words or the paired terms genus and species.

rubric.why: Award for a correct convention for writing scientific names.
rubric.description: The genus begins with a capital letter and the species name with a lowercase letter; the name is italicised or underlined when handwritten.
rubric.how: Look for correct capitalisation or italic/underlining convention.

modelAnswer: Binomial nomenclature is the system of giving each organism a two-word scientific name: the genus name and the species name.
The genus begins with a capital letter and the species name with a lowercase letter; the name is italicised or underlined when handwritten.

items.followUp: State two characteristics of organisms placed in kingdom Protista.

rubric.why: Award for describing Monera as prokaryotic and generally unicellular.
rubric.description: Kingdom Monera consists of prokaryotic, mostly unicellular organisms.
rubric.how: Look for prokaryotic/no true nucleus and unicellular.

rubric.why: Award for naming examples of Monera.
rubric.description: Examples include bacteria and cyanobacteria (blue-green algae).
rubric.how: Look for bacteria and/or cyanobacteria as examples.

modelAnswer: Kingdom Monera consists of prokaryotic, mostly unicellular organisms that lack a true nucleus.
It includes bacteria and cyanobacteria (blue-green algae).

items.followUp: What occurs during the S phase of the cell cycle?

rubric.why: Award for locating G1 in the cell cycle.
rubric.description: G1 is the first gap phase of interphase, after mitosis and before the S phase.
rubric.how: Look for its position after mitosis and before DNA synthesis/S phase, or identification as the first gap of interphase.

rubric.why: Award for describing cell growth and preparation for DNA replication.
rubric.description: During G1 the cell grows, makes proteins and organelles, and prepares for DNA replication.
rubric.how: Look for cell growth and a preparation activity such as protein/organelle production or preparation for DNA replication.

modelAnswer: G1 is the first gap phase of interphase, occurring after mitosis and before the S phase.
During G1, the cell grows, makes proteins and organelles, and prepares for DNA replication.

items.followUp: What is crossing over, and during which stage of meiosis does it occur?

rubric.why: Award for identifying chiasmata as crossing points between homologous non-sister chromatids.
rubric.description: Chiasmata are the points where non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes cross.
rubric.how: Look for crossing between homologous chromosomes or non-sister chromatids.

rubric.why: Award for linking chiasmata to crossing over and the exchange of genetic material during prophase I.
rubric.description: At chiasmata, crossing over allows exchange of genetic material during prophase I of meiosis.
rubric.how: Look for crossing over or genetic-material exchange, preferably located in prophase I.

modelAnswer: Chiasmata are the points where non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes cross.
At these points, crossing over exchanges genetic material during prophase I of meiosis.

items.followUp: Describe how a new individual forms by budding in yeast.

rubric.why: Award for describing formation and growth of a bud on the Hydra parent.
rubric.description: Repeated mitotic cell division in the body wall produces a small outgrowth or bud on the parent Hydra.
rubric.how: Look for a bud/outgrowth forming on the parent, with cell division or growth.

rubric.why: Award for describing development of the bud and its separation as a new Hydra.
rubric.description: The bud develops a mouth and tentacles, then detaches from the parent and lives independently.
rubric.how: Look for development of structures and eventual separation/independent life.

modelAnswer: Repeated mitotic cell division in the body wall of Hydra forms a small outgrowth called a bud.
The bud grows and develops a mouth and tentacles; it then detaches from the parent and lives independently.
